source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline, CHI
finding: Original human test of asking why did and why didn't questions. Alice users with the tool debugged far faster and finished more tasks.
numbers: Six identical scenarios: debugging time cut by average factor 7.8 (F1,5=12.64, p<.02). Tasks done in 90 min: 3.20 (SD .457) with vs 2.25 (SD .500) without, t(7)=3.0, p<.02 = 40% more. Small N: 4 without, 5 with (CMU HCI masters students).
quote: Interrogative Debugging is a new debugging paradigm in which programmers can ask why did and even why didn't questions
limits: Tiny sample, Alice (a novice 3D environment), only 6 comparable scenarios, iterative tool design between sessions (usefulness rose from 0 of 3 to 5 of 5 questions).
agent_relevance: Our agent can ask a causal question about the failure and get an answer from the run trace instead of guessing causes in code. This is O5 in human form.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline: question statistics
finding: From earlier Alice studies: programmers' own questions were mostly why-not, and about code that might plausibly have run.
numbers: 68% of questions were why didn't, rest why did. 85% concerned one object. Whyline useful for 19 of 24 questions. Why-didn't questions 17, 19, 16 per study vs why-did 8, 5, 3.
limits: Alice only. One user said the tool was 'useless' when he could not ask a why-didn't question.
agent_relevance: Support the negative question 'why did X not happen' in the agent: missing events are common and hard for plain tools.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging Reinvented, ICSE (Java Whyline)
finding: Java Whyline answers why-did and why-didn't questions using static and dynamic slicing plus a call graph. Novices with it beat experts without it on one task.
numbers: Median 4 min (range 1-12) with Whyline vs 10 min (range 3-38) without; p<.05 Wilcoxon rank sums. Whyline users more than 2x faster; most were self-described novices. Unpublished follow-up on ArgoUML: experts with Whyline 'twice as successful in half the time' (preliminary).
quote: Novice programmers with the Whyline were twice as fast as expert programmers without it.
limits: Only one task in the main test. Trace-based: impractical for runs longer than a few minutes or heavy data; heavier setup than a breakpoint debugger. ArgoUML result is preliminary and unpublished.
agent_relevance: Backward explanation from an output is cheap when a trace exists. Give the agent an execution trace tool, not only source.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging Reinvented: tracing limits
finding: Trace cost measured on five open-source Java programs (binclock, jTidy, javac, jEdit, ArgoUML). Tracing slows runs and memory grows with trace size.
numbers: Largest tested trace: ArgoUML with 35,597 I/O events over about a minute of use; traced runs several times slower than untraced.
limits: Prototype timings on 2008 hardware.
agent_relevance: Tracing has a real cost; the agent loop should use short targeted runs.

source: Ko and Myers (2005) framework for causes of software errors (cognitive breakdowns)
finding: Framework of chains of cognitive breakdowns; the Whyline was derived from it. Abstract restates the factor-of-8 and 40% results.
numbers: Abstract: debugging time reduced by a factor of 8, programmers get 40% further.
limits: Restates the 2004 study; not independent.
agent_relevance: Shows the origin: the tool attacks wrong hypotheses, not typing speed.

source: Ko, Aung, Myers (2007) Information needs in collocated software development teams, ICSE
finding: Observation of 17 developers in 90-minute sessions. The most often deferred searches were about program behavior: why code was written so, and the cause of a program state.
numbers: 17 developers, 90-min logs, 21 information types.
quote: The most often deferred searches included knowledge about design and program behavior
limits: Observational; one large company; deferral shows unmet need, not wrong answers.
agent_relevance: Cause-of-state questions are the unmet need that a why-tool or a why-prompt targets.

source: Weiser (1982) Programmers use slices when debugging, CACM
finding: Founding slicing study: debugging programmers mentally follow statements that can influence the faulty value. NOT opened this session; ACM page returned only an HTML stub.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not read; check before use.
agent_relevance: Backward slice from the wrong value is the old human strategy behind O5.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers? ISSTA
finding: User study of whether ranked fault-location lists help real programmers. NOT opened (HTTP 403). From memory it found weak or no benefit; verify.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Boundary: location lists did not clearly help humans, which fits Alaboudi 2020 where locations did not help but hypotheses did.

source: Khakzad Shahandashti et al. (2024) Program Slicing in the Era of Large Language Models
finding: GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Llama-2, Gemma-7B on static and dynamic slicing of 100 Java LeetCode programs. Models get dependencies partly right but almost never the exact slice.
numbers: GPT-4o best: static Accuracy-D 60.84% (one-shot CoT), Accuracy-EM 7.33%; dynamic Accuracy-D 59.69% (zero-shot), EM 0%. GPT-3.5 46.43%, Gemma-7B 43.43%, Llama-2 17.57% (static best). NS-Slicer CodeBERT 60.52% D, 0% EM. Each run 3 times, averaged.
limits: Java only, small programs; few-shot effects inconsistent (GPT-4o dynamic: one-shot 41.77%, one-shot CoT 58.62%). Commonest failure cause: complex control flow; commonest location: variable declarations and assignments.
agent_relevance: LLM backward slicing by reasoning alone is unreliable: let code compute the slice (G2), use the model to read and judge it.

source: Khakzad Shahandashti et al. (2024) slicing: prompt fixes
finding: Two taxonomy-guided fixes helped a little: refined prompts, and iterative prompting with feedback on failure cause and location.
numbers: Prompt crafting +4% accuracy; iterative prompting +3.9%.
limits: Small gains; the feedback needs ground truth location, so it is not usable in real runs.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording alone will not make a model slice well; use external computation.

source: Chang et al. (2025) SliceMate: static slicing via LLM agents
finding: Three LLM agents (synthesis, verification, refinement) build slices without a dependency graph. Tested on SliceBench: 2,200 hand-annotated Java and Python programs, 5 to 8,577 lines.
numbers: Versus best baseline: accuracy up to +22%, F1 up to +28%. Small programs: F1 +31.5%, accuracy +37%, exact match +62.6%. Large programs: F1 +62.5%, accuracy +63.1%, exact match +6%.
limits: Authors' own benchmark; traditional baselines fail on incomplete code.
agent_relevance: A generate, verify, repair loop for a backward slice is a pattern for the agent: separate checks for completeness and conciseness.

source: Chang et al. (2025) SliceMate: downstream bug localization
finding: Slices from SliceMate fed to two bug-localization tools raise Top-N, so slicing context helps localization.
numbers: BugsInPy IncBL Top-1/3/5/10 = 0.19/0.43/0.57/0.70 (gain over best baseline slicer +5/+24/+32/+34 pts). LLM4FPM 0.08/0.21/0.39/0.70. Defects4J IncBL 0.13/0.22/0.35/0.52; LLM4FPM 0.11/0.32/0.51/0.75. Debugging bug coverage up to +12% over best baseline.
limits: Gains are largest at Top-10 and small at Top-1: slicing narrows the candidate set but does not pick the winner.
agent_relevance: Slicing is a filter. Use it to shrink the search before the model chooses.

source: Pei et al. (2025) RecovSlicing: LLM as execution estimator
finding: Answers 'why does this variable have this value' (dynamic data dependency) from a partial trace plus code, by letting an LLM estimate the missing execution. Beats classic slicers on three benchmarks.
numbers: 8,300 data dependencies, 3 benchmarks. Accuracy 80.3%, 91.1%, 98.3% vs best baseline 39.0%, 82.0%, 59.9%. Baseline recall 53.4%, 79.1%, 87.1%. Variable recovery precision 91.48%, recall 89.24%; definition inference 83.24%. In-context learning adds 5-7%. Stable across GPT-4o and Gemma-3. In regression localization finds 16% more regressions than Tregression.
quote: Dynamic data dependency, answering the question of why the variable has this value
limits: Non-deterministic LLM; needs partial instrumentation; Java.
agent_relevance: Record a cheap partial trace and let the LLM fill gaps. This is the 'why' question exactly.

source: Robustness of LLM fault localization to semantic-preserving mutations (ICST 2026; authors not recorded)
finding: LLMs localize injected faults; then the program is rewritten without changing its meaning. Models often lose the fault, so they lean on surface cues.
numbers: 10 LLMs, 750,013 FL tasks, 1,300+ Java and Python programs. After semantic-preserving mutation 78% of earlier correct localizations failed. Misleading variable names hurt least (29.02% accuracy). Faults in first quarter of code found most often. Reasoning and multimodal models (Claude, Gemini) best; longitudinal gain Gemini +1.8%, Claude +1.0%.
limits: Injected, not natural, faults; specifications supplied.
agent_relevance: Do not trust one localization; re-test under a rewritten view of the code and check agreement.

source: Liu et al. (2026) BluesFL: block-level instruction-oriented slicing, DAC 2026
finding: Slicing along the executed instruction path guides an LLM through 19K lines of SystemVerilog RISC-V code, like an engineer would.
numbers: 24 bugs correct at Top-1 vs 7 for prior best (+242.9%). $0.257 per bug. Ablation: without instruction path the LLM visits uncovered blocks and gives false positives; without signal values it checks 88.3 blocks instead of 15.4 and cost rises 609% ($0.257 to $1.821).
limits: Hardware code, one core, small bug count; backends GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet.
agent_relevance: Restricting the model to the executed path and giving observed values cuts search and cost by large factors.

source: Levin et al. (2025) ChatDBG, FSE
finding: An LLM given control of GDB/LLDB/pdb answers why-questions of the live program ('why is x null?'), then reports cause and fix. Has a backward slice command for notebooks (via ipyflow).
numbers: Python student bugs: plain 'why?' fixed 57%; error-specific question 67%; one follow-up dialog step 85%. C/C++ crashes: root cause diagnosed in virtually all trials; 36% of fixes hit root cause, 55% only the proximate cause. LLM issues 0-12 commands per run, mostly info, slice, p.
quote: ChatDBG can successfully analyze root causes, explain bugs, and generate accurate fixes
limits: Small student programs; success judged by authors; C/C++ fixes often only proximate.
agent_relevance: Strong support: the why question, tool autonomy and a follow-up turn each raised success. Backward slice is offered as an agent tool.

source: Levin et al. (2025) ChatDBG ablation (RQ2)
finding: Every component helped; largest gains from taking the wheel (tool autonomy), user context about expected behaviour, and multi-step dialog.
numbers: 57% plain, 67% specialised, 85% with one more turn (RQ1). Per-component bars only in Figure 7 (not extracted).
limits: Student labs.
agent_relevance: Add a second turn that re-asks with the gap in the first answer.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) AutoFL: explainable fault localization with LLM navigation
finding: LLM navigates code through function calls from one failing test and explains why a spot is suspicious. Repeating runs gives a confidence signal.
numbers: Method-level acc@1 over Ochiai SBFL: +19.7% Defects4J, +166.7% BugsInPy (GPT-3.5); +233.3% BugsInPy with GPT-4. Confidence vs precision@1 Spearman +0.57 (Defects4J), +0.52 (BugsInPy), 5 reruns. Of 300 sampled explanations from 60 bugs, about 20% accurately describe how the bug happened; 56.7% of bugs had an accurate description.
limits: GPT-3.5 lagged SBFL at acc@3 and acc@5 on BugsInPy.
agent_relevance: Ask for a reason, not only a location; use agreement across reruns as a confidence measure.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) AutoFL: developer interviews
finding: Developers supported explained localization (the paper cites ~90% rating rationales important) but redundant text and wrong fix suggestions could mislead.
numbers: Interviews with professional developers; they wanted a few explanations, not many.
limits: Qualitative, small sample.
agent_relevance: Output one short causal chain, not a list.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) LDB: debugging with runtime execution (ACL)
finding: Splits a program into basic blocks and shows variable values after each block; the LLM checks each block against the task, like stepping in a debugger.
numbers: Up to +9.8% over baseline on HumanEval, MBPP, TransCoder across backbones; up to 98.2% HumanEval with Reflexion seeds and a stronger debugging backbone. Beats Self-Debugging (dry run or explain).
limits: Function-level benchmarks, not repositories; GPT-3.5 main backbone.
agent_relevance: Real values from execution beat the model's imagined dry run; feed observed state per step.

source: Liu et al. (2024) REval: reasoning runtime behavior of a program
finding: Tests whether code LLMs predict runtime behaviour (output, path, coverage, state) and stay consistent.
numbers: Average accuracy on Runtime Behavior Reasoning 44.4% across models; average Incremental Consistency score 10.3. Best GPT-4-Turbo: 75.0% accuracy, IC 42.5 (more than 21.9 above others).
limits: HumanEval-style programs; IC metric is the authors' own.
agent_relevance: Models cannot reliably run code in their head, so a backward chain built on guessed execution breaks. Observe, do not simulate.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet? ICLR
finding: Self-repair is limited by the model's feedback on its own failing code. A human explaining the bug raises repair a lot.
numbers: GPT-4 repair success with GPT-4 feedback 33.30% overall vs 52.60% with human feedback (introductory 42.64 vs 62.21; interview 19.33 vs 45.67; competition 3.67 vs 14.67). With cost counted, self-repair gains are modest, sometimes absent.
limits: Small human-feedback study; APPS and HumanEval.
agent_relevance: The bottleneck is the diagnosis (why it fails), which is the Whyline question. Better causal explanations beat more repair rounds.

source: Lee et al. (2025) debug-gym: interactive debugging environment
finding: Gives agents a pdb tool: rewrite only, debug (pdb from start), debug(5) (pdb after 5 rewrites). Debugger gave modest gains, large only for the strongest models.
numbers: SWE-bench-Lite success rewrite/debug/debug(5): GPT-4o 19.1/17.2/23.6; o3-mini 8.5/22.1/19.8; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 37.2/48.4/52.1; Llama 3.3-70B 2.4/4.0/4.8; 4o-mini 4.0/3.5/6.2. Aider (simple code gen): no clear effect. 3 runs each.
quote: still far from being proficient debuggers
limits: Minimal prompt agents; authors blame scarce debugging traces in training data. Weaker models do not use pdb well.
agent_relevance: A debugger tool is not enough; the model must ask good questions of it. Starting without it and adding it after failed rewrites was often best.

source: Lee et al. (2025) debug-gym: Mini-nightmare trace
finding: On the patcher task weaker models loop on rewriting the same parsing code; Claude 3.7 and R1-Distill-Llama-70B spotted the line-number range problem. A Claude trace looked human: view files, break, print variables, clear break, one rewrite.
numbers: Mini-nightmare: 10 hand-made buggy programs, about 40 lines each.
limits: Anecdotal trace, 3 runs.
agent_relevance: Target behaviour: form a hypothesis from observed values, then make one targeted edit.

source: Chang et al. (2025) BugCerberus hierarchical bug localization
finding: Three LLMs at file, function and statement levels use program-dependence context including backward and forward slices from candidate code.
numbers: SWE-bench-Lite statement-level Top-N (1,3,5,10) beats SOTA by 16.5%, 5.4%, 10.2%, 23.1%; raises Agentless fix rate by 17.4%.
limits: Fine-tuned models; abstract numbers only.
agent_relevance: Better localization raises end fix rate, so spend effort on the backward step.

source: Ko and Myers (2008): contrast with Delta Debugging
finding: Paper positions the Whyline against Delta Debugging and differential diagnosis: those need a pass/fail spec and runs, while the Whyline lets the user ask any question.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Conceptual.
agent_relevance: Both useful: question-driven for open diagnosis, delta-style for minimal failing input.
